The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨-1,1⟩$ and $b=⟨2,-2⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,-2)-f(-1,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,-2⟩-⟨-1,1⟩) \\ ((-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+1)-({1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩ \\ 9-3 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩ \\ 6 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,2y⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},2{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩ \\ 6 & =⟨2{c}_{1},2{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩ \\ 6 & =6{c}_{1}-6{c}_{2} \\ 1 & ={c}_{1}-{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{-2-1} & =\frac{x-(-1)}{2-(-1)} \\ \frac{y-1}{(-3)} & =\frac{x+1}{3} \\ y-1 & =-(x+1) \\ y & =-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =-{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the equation ${c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=1,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-(-{c}_{1}) & =1 \\ 2{c}_{1} & =1 \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find ${c}_{2}=-{c}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}).$
